note: The plain case: one streamable-http remote over https, no headers, nothing to fill in.
Literal header values are fine — they carry no credential and every install sends the same bytes.
The publisher extension point declares OAuth; the summary reports it as a hint, and no secret rides the document.
Two remotes offered; the first streamable-http one is picked and the event-stream sibling is ignored.
A package-only bundle: no address at all, one npm package at one exact version. An environment slot DECLARED secret is metadata — the machine that runs the server fills it, and no credential travels.
The same shape from the other common registry, with the official STRUCTURED arguments — a named flag carrying a literal value and a positional naming its hint.
An OCI package pins itself inside the identifier, by digest. The 64 hex characters are an integrity digest, not a credential — the belt reads what precedes them.
An MCPB download is identified by the sha-256 of its file; the hash under a fileSha256 key is likewise integrity, not a secret.
Both ways offered at once. The summary still reports the placed remote; the packages ride along for the machines that prefer one.
The npm grammar read positively still takes everything semver spells: a prerelease tail and build metadata are part of one exact version.
The same for the other grammar — a PEP 440 release candidate names exactly one released version, so it publishes.
A bare wildcard is no range spelling anyone lists, and npm resolves it to whatever is current on the day each machine installs.
A dist-tag reads like a word and moves like a pointer: the version has to match the registry's own grammar, not merely avoid the range spellings.
A range resolves to whatever the day supplies — two machines installing the same bundle would not get the same bytes.
`latest` is the moving pointer the registry reserves, and reads as a version only until it moves.
An OCI reference carries its version in the identifier, so a `latest` tag there is the same unpinned promise.
A tag that reads like a version is still a movable label: the publisher can point 3.0.0 at other bytes tomorrow, and two machines a week apart would run different code.
An MCPB download with no fileSha256 is a URL whose contents can change under it — nothing to check the arriving bytes against.
A slot NAMED for a credential is fine; the same slot with the value already in it is somebody's credential travelling to every machine.
The name says nothing and the entropy belt sees an ordinary word, but the document itself says the slot is secret — and it arrives filled in. The publisher's own word outranks every heuristic.
The name says nothing, the value reads as a generated key: the credential scan reads package environment values exactly as it reads header ones.
The registry format spells arguments as objects that state their own type; a bare string array is a different format's shape.
transport is one of the three fields the schema requires — without it nothing knows how the installed server is spoken to.
The server's own version is held to the same rule as a package's: one version, never a moving pointer.
Only the event-stream transport is offered, and no packages: there is nothing this can place.
No remotes and no packages reads exactly like sse-only: nothing to hand an agent.
Plain http would put every call and every reply on the wire in the clear.
A {placeholder} in the URL means the document is not yet an address — someone has to fill it in per machine.
isSecret says out loud that the value is a credential; a shared bundle never carries one.
A required header with no literal value is a credential slot by another name.
Per-installation variables make the header something each machine fills in — the same slot again.
A literal value that has the shape of a token: the flag was omitted, the credential was not.
The credential rides the query string instead of a header; the scan reads the whole document, so it lands the same way.
name is required — it is the identity the catalog and the registry lane both key on.
The grammar is exactly one slash between a reverse-DNS namespace and a server name.
description is capped at 100 characters.
version is required; without it there is nothing to compare a later publish against.
Not JSON at all — the commonest paste mistake, refused before anything is read out of it.

200 nested containers. serde_json refuses past 127 levels (its default recursion limit), and the web gate caps at the same depth explicitly — one verdict, both languages, no stack overflow either side.
The scheme is case-insensitive: HTTPS:// is the same https the gate requires.
The token is spelled entirely in \uXXXX escapes, so the raw text never shows it — the scan over the DECODED strings does.
Authorization is a credential-bearing header NAME — refused whatever the value looks like, flags and entropy aside.
userinfo in the endpoint URL is a credential in the address itself.
An https prefix does not make an address: the host carries spaces, which no URL parser accepts.
No host at all — https:// followed by a query is not an address.
One invalid UTF-8 byte inside a string: a lossy decode would parse it, so both gates must decode STRICTLY and refuse.
An MCP candidate may hold exactly server.json and README.md — any other file refuses, naming the allowed set.

note: Every allowed file's bytes run the credential scan — a token in the README refuses exactly like one in the document.
The placed remote is clean and a sibling carries a password in its address — every remotes[] entry travels in the same bytes, so every one of them is judged.
A credential-bearing header on a remote that is not the one being placed: sharing it is exactly as wide, so the header rules run over every entry too.
A header declaring an empty variables block is still a per-machine fill-in — and the placement engine refuses it, so a bundle carrying one would publish and never land.
A brace pair in a header value is the header's own template: somebody fills it in per machine, which is the one thing shared bytes cannot carry.
A real model-provider key in a header value: the left boundary the sk- shape now wears does not weaken it, because a key never starts mid-word.
Hyphenated prose is not a credential: a server named task-management-and-scheduling holds sk- mid-word, and the shape's left boundary is what tells the two apart.

https:example.com/mcp is an address to one URL parser (which supplies the slashes) and nothing at all to the other — so neither tier reads it, and a document spelling it can never be published and then land.

A backslash in the authority: one parser ends the host at it and sees no userinfo, the other reads h\ as a user name. The shape refuses before either reading is taken, so both tiers answer the same code.
A tab inside the host is deleted by one parser before it parses and refused outright by the other. An address whose meaning depends on who reads it is not one.
A digest is 64 hex characters, so the carve-out demands 64 hex characters: typing sha256: in front of a generated key exempts nothing.
The same closing on the other spelling — a fileSha256 key is a name a publisher chooses, and the value under it has to be a whole digest to be read as one.
A description of 84 characters that occupies 134 UTF-16 units: the ceiling counts CHARACTERS on both tiers, so an emoji costs one wherever it is measured.
